text:
Keep the Joins: Why Primary Schools Should Still Teach Joined-Up Handwriting

Every few years someone proposes that joined-up handwriting should go the way of the slate and the inkwell. The case sounds like common sense. Children will spend their adult lives typing, dictating and tapping, and curriculum time is scarce. Finland made cursive optional in 2016. The American Common Core standards left it out in 2010. Why should a seven-year-old spend hours learning to loop an f into an l when she could be learning to code, or simply to read?

I think the abolitionists are wrong, and that primary schools should carry on teaching children to join their letters. Tradition is a poor reason, and so is the claim that cursive is beautiful, though it can be. The reason that matters is practical: fluent handwriting is still one of the cheapest and most effective tools a child has for thinking on paper, and joining is how most children's handwriting becomes fluent.

Start with what is not in dispute. Writing by hand matters for learning, and the evidence for that has grown stronger as screens have spread. Brain-imaging work by Karin James and colleagues found that when pre-literate children formed letters by hand, they later showed activity in the brain's reading network when looking at those letters, which children who had typed or traced them did not. EEG studies from Audrey van der Meer's lab in Norway found more widespread brain connectivity during handwriting than during typing, in patterns associated with memory and learning. Forming a letter is a more demanding act than pressing a key, because the hand has to build the shape; on a keyboard every letter is the same movement in a different place. That effort appears to help fix letters, and then spellings, in memory.

None of that is specifically an argument for joined-up writing, and honest defenders of cursive should say so. The studies compare the hand with the keyboard, not print script with joined script. Direct comparisons between the two styles are fewer and more mixed. So the argument for the joins has to be made on other ground, and I think it can be.

The first ground is fluency. The largest obstacle to a young child's writing is the mechanical one. A child who has to think about how to form each letter has little attention left for what she wants to say. Decades of research by Steve Graham, Virginia Berninger and others show that handwriting automaticity predicts the length and quality of children's compositions, and that teaching handwriting explicitly improves their writing, the content as well as the neatness. Working memory is limited, and whatever is spent on the pencil is unavailable for the sentence.

Joined writing is a technology for automaticity. Print script requires the pen to be lifted, repositioned and restarted dozens of times per line, and each restart is a small decision about where to begin. A joined hand turns a word into one continuous movement. This is why adult handwriting, left to itself, almost always drifts toward joining: people who were only ever taught print invent their own ligatures, because lifting the pen is slow. The fastest writers in Graham's well-known study of older pupils were those using a mixed hand, mostly joined with a few pragmatic lifts, and that is exactly what good teaching of joins produces by the end of primary school. If children are going to join anyway, it is better to teach them efficient joins than to leave each child to improvise bad ones.

The second ground is spelling. A joined word is learned as a single motor pattern, and frequent letter strings such as -ing, -tion and -ough become gestures the hand knows. Teachers have long observed that children "feel" a misspelling when the movement goes wrong, and some intervention studies support this: a Canadian study by Marie-France Morin and colleagues found that pupils taught cursive from the start made better progress in spelling and syntax than those taught print or both styles in sequence. The evidence is not overwhelming, but it points in one direction. Joining also solves a problem every infant teacher knows, which is spacing. In print, the gap between letters and the gap between words differ only in degree, and young children muddle them. In a joined hand, a word is the thing that is connected, and its boundary is visible.

The third ground is the pupils for whom writing is hardest. Many dyslexia specialists favour teaching a continuous joined hand. Each letter starts in the same place, on the line, which removes a decision. Letters that mirror each other in print, b and d, p and q, are formed with quite different movements in joined script and are harder to reverse. The rhythm of the whole word reinforces the sequence of its letters. The research base here is thinner than practitioners' confidence might suggest, but the reasoning is sound and the classroom experience is extensive. A reform sold as relief for struggling children would take away something that helps many of them.

The fourth ground is bluntly practical. In England, and in most education systems, the examinations that decide a young person's options are still written by hand, against the clock. A sixteen-year-old sitting GCSEs will write for many hours over a few weeks. A pupil with a slow, effortful print hand is at a real disadvantage: she writes less, tires sooner, and has less attention for the argument. Perhaps exams will move on screen within a decade, though that has been predicted for longer than a decade. A primary school teaching a five-year-old today cannot bet her exam results on that. And beyond exams, the pen is not disappearing from classrooms. Notes, annotations, working in mathematics, diagrams and plans are still done by hand because paper is quick, flexible and free of distraction. The widely cited finding that longhand note-takers understand lectures better than laptop note-takers has not replicated cleanly, but nobody has shown the reverse, and few teachers who have faced a room of open laptops doubt which medium holds attention better.

Now the objections. The strongest is opportunity cost: time spent on loops is time not spent on something else. But the cost is routinely overstated. Good handwriting teaching is ten or fifteen minutes a day in the early years, tapering to occasional practice, and it is usually combined with spelling, so the same minutes serve both. And if the automaticity research is right, the supposed rival for those minutes, writing itself, is the main beneficiary. The time is an investment in every later lesson that involves a pencil.

The second objection is that children should learn to type instead. They should learn to type, as well. Touch-typing is a valuable skill and schools teach it badly or not at all. But it does not substitute at age six. Young children's hands are small, keyboards are built for adults, and the evidence suggests typing does less than handwriting for letter learning at the stage when letters are being learned. The sensible sequence is hand first, keyboard added in the junior years. The choice between them is a false one.

The third objection is that print is enough: teach a clear, unjoined hand and stop. This is the most reasonable form of the opposing case, and it is roughly what Finland chose. My answer is that it stops just short of the payoff. Children taught only print either stay slow or invent their own joins, with inefficient movements that are hard to unlearn. Having taught the letter shapes, the further cost of teaching the joins is small, and the gain is speed and stamina for the next ten years of schooling. Many schools now reduce the cost further by teaching letters with exit strokes from the start, so that joining is a natural next step and no second alphabet has to be learned.

There is a lesser argument I will mention without leaning on it. A child who cannot write a joined hand generally struggles to read one, and so is cut off from a grandparent's letters, a parish register or a soldier's diary. That is a real loss, and it helped persuade a number of American states, California among them in 2023, to bring cursive back after a decade without it. But access to old manuscripts would not justify the teaching time on its own.

What does justify it is that writing is thinking, and for children the hand is still the main route from thought to page. Joined handwriting is the mature form of that skill, the point at which the mechanics stop demanding attention. Schools should teach it sensibly: without fetishising copperplate, without penalising a child whose fluent hand is partly unjoined, and without the hours of joyless drill that gave handwriting lessons a bad name. But they should teach it. The children who would lose most from dropping it are the ones with the least fluency to spare.
